title: The 10 Commandments of Wall Street. Goldman Sachs 101: 28-Minute Crash Course (Part 2)
summary: Part 2 of the hosts dissecting the ten rules Jean received on her first day at Goldman Sachs University 15 years ago, covering rules 6 through 10: seek consensus, seek out and manage mentors, attention to detail, ask questions rather than assume, and first impressions last. The hosts translate each into tactical practices, from back-channeling before decision meetings and follow-up email templates to the visual-verbal-vocal formula for first impressions.

ideas.idea: Decisions are not made in the decision-making meeting; walk in already knowing with 85%+ confidence how every person in the room will vote and why.
ideas.detail: Goldman rule 6, 'seek consensus and input from colleagues', in practice means back-channeling: one-on-one conversations to vet your idea in a low-stakes setting and address objections before the high-stakes meeting. Cherie calls it one of the dirty secrets of office politics that the top 1% of performers use, and says public corporate interactions are largely orchestrated.

ideas.idea: The best way to get people on board is to make them part of the idea, ideally so they feel it was partly their idea that you are executing on their behalf.
ideas.detail: Brainstorm sessions often serve this purpose: leaders enter with an agenda but the meeting lets participants feel their ideas matter, which is a balance of both.

ideas.idea: Come to every mentor coffee chat with a prepared list of roughly ten things to discuss and why this person specifically is the one to ask.
ideas.detail: Goldman rule 7 is 'seek out mentors and manage them'; time is the only resource you cannot get more of, so respect it by preparing for five minutes, arriving on time and having looked at their LinkedIn profile.

ideas.idea: Follow up within 15 minutes of a coffee chat with a specific thank-you: name one thing you took away and how you will apply it.
ideas.detail: Template: 'Thanks so much for your time, I really enjoyed our conversation, especially XYZ, and I'm going to apply it in ABC way.' ChatGPT can help; the small touchpoint makes mentors feel heard and is what managing relationships means. Jean admits her Goldman-bred perfectionism makes her procrastinate such emails.

ideas.idea: Attention to detail is the analyst's entire job because senior people zoom out on strategy and depend on juniors for accuracy on decisions worth hundreds of millions.
ideas.topic: Finance industry: VC, PE, banking, hedge funds
ideas.detail: Goldman rule 8, 'someone will notice'; Jean's group managed hundreds of billions and now about a trillion dollars, and a missed comma could cost a client. Juniors who focus on details get rewarded.

ideas.idea: Goldman's perfection culture was somewhat self-important: nobody dies if an internal memo has a typo, yet everyone was stressed to the point of exhaustion.
ideas.topic: Finance industry: VC, PE, banking, hedge funds
ideas.detail: At 21 Jean believed CEO Lloyd Blankfein's line that they were doing 'God's work'; even documents for the same 30 colleagues had to be perfect, which she says explains why it still takes her so long to write an email.

ideas.idea: Ask the dumb questions; assuming is dangerous and pretending to know makes you a 'midwit' who makes wrong decisions.
ideas.detail: Goldman rule 9. Cherie grew up scared to question authority and held her tongue in high school and college classrooms, but over the last decade adopted 'go max dumb', a phrase from Season 3 guest Vu Tran; the right people respect a smart person asking basic questions.

ideas.idea: There is such a thing as a stupid question: one that has already been asked and answered to you, so carry a notebook, write the answer down and never ask twice.
ideas.detail: Jean's addendum to rule 9; a clarifying re-ask ('could you explain it another way?') is fine, but repeating the same question because you did not listen disrespects the other person's time.

ideas.idea: Taking notes during an informational coffee chat is so rare that it can get you hired.
ideas.detail: Cherie prepared questions from Albert's LinkedIn, wrote down his answers in a notebook and sent a follow-up email; after she joined his team he told her nobody had ever written down anything he said and that was when he knew he wanted her.

ideas.idea: First impressions form in the first 30 seconds from three Vs, visual, verbal and vocal, and much of it happens before you open your mouth.
ideas.detail: Goldman rule 10, 'first impressions last a long time', combined with a Stanford GSB communications lecture: how you dress and hold yourself, what you say, and how you say it. Cherie adds a fourth V, vibes. You get one shot and impressions are hard to change.

ideas.idea: Being smart and working hard is not enough; you must present well and look put together to be taken seriously and put in front of clients.
ideas.detail: Jean says this lesson took her 15 years because she grew up believing her worth was her mind and grades; a Zynga manager, Harvey, once asked whether she had brushed her hair after a 3am night, the first time anyone had commented on her appearance.

ideas.idea: If your family did not teach you presentation skills like hair and makeup, learn them intentionally on your own, the way the Kardashians' father paid for professional makeup lessons when the girls hit their teens.
ideas.detail: The hosts' mom invested heavily in skincare, a generational benefit, but wore little makeup, so Cherie learned the smokey eye at 13 from Michelle Phan YouTube tutorials.
